text:
The Joined-Up Case: Why Primary Schools Should Keep Teaching Cursive

Every few years someone declares joined-up handwriting obsolete. Children will type, the argument goes, or dictate, or tap on glass, so why spend hours drilling the loop of a "b" into the letter after it? The question sounds reasonable. Schools have little time, and keeping a skill that looks antique can seem like nostalgia passed off as teaching. But the case for dropping joined-up writing rests on a misunderstanding of what handwriting is for and what it does for the children learning it. Primary schools should keep teaching it. They should not teach it as calligraphy or as a moral virtue. They should teach it as the most efficient and durable form of a skill that children still need every school day.

**Handwriting has not gone away**

Start with a fact that the "obsolete" argument tends to skip: children in primary school spend a large share of their day writing by hand. They write in exercise books, on worksheets and on whiteboards, and in many systems they sit handwritten exams well into secondary school. A child who cannot write quickly and legibly is not just missing an old-fashioned skill. They are held back in almost every subject, because the physical act of writing uses up attention that should go to thinking.

This is the first and most practical argument for joining. Print, where each letter is formed separately with the pen lifted between them, is slower for most fluent writers. Every lift and repositioning costs a small amount of time and a small amount of motor planning. Joined writing, done well, removes many of those breaks and lets the hand move continuously across the line. Lifting the pen once is trivial. Doing it hundreds of times on a page adds up, and the cost grows over a school career. A ten-year-old asked to write a story in forty minutes gets more of their ideas onto the page if the mechanics are fast and automatic.

The point is not speed for its own sake. Educational psychologists have long described writing as a juggling act. The writer has to keep the idea, the sentence, the spelling and the letter formation in mind at once, and working memory is limited. When forming letters takes conscious effort, less capacity is left for composition. Researchers such as Virginia Berninger have argued for years that handwriting fluency in the early years is linked to the quality and length of what children compose, not just to how neat it looks. A joined style that becomes automatic frees the mind for what matters: what the child is trying to say.

**The brain and the pen**

There is also a growing body of research suggesting that writing by hand engages the brain differently from typing. Studies using EEG, including work by Audrey van der Meer and colleagues in Norway, have found broader patterns of brain connectivity when participants write by hand than when they type, patterns the researchers link to memory and learning. Separately, work on note-taking, most famously Mueller and Oppenheimer's 2014 paper "The Pen Is Mightier Than the Keyboard", suggested that students who take notes by hand process the material more deeply than those who type, though later replications have been mixed.

This evidence should be treated with care. Much of it compares handwriting in general with typing, not joined-up writing with print, and some findings have not held up cleanly. But it undermines the idea that handwriting is a quaint skill that technology has replaced like for like. If forming letters by hand helps children remember and learn letter shapes and words, then teaching a fluent, efficient form of handwriting is worth the time. It should not be the first thing cut.

There is a more specific argument too. Many teachers and some specialists hold that joined writing supports spelling, because common letter strings ("-ing", "-tion", "th", "ough") are produced as single continuous movements. The hand learns the word as a pattern as well as the eye. The research here is less settled than the general case for handwriting fluency, and advocates should not overstate it. Still, it fits with what experienced teachers report, and it is consistent with the wider evidence that motor learning and literacy are connected.

**Answering the case against**

The opponents of cursive make real points, and an honest argument has to meet them.

The first objection is that it is a waste of time in a crowded curriculum. Finland drew headlines in 2016 when it stopped requiring joined-up handwriting and put more emphasis on keyboard skills. But teaching joined writing does not need a separate, lengthy programme. In England, for instance, the national curriculum expects children to start joining in the early junior years, and good schools build it into the daily handwriting practice that already exists. The choice is not between cursive and coding. It is between finishing handwriting instruction properly and leaving it half done. Typing should be taught as well. The two skills do not compete for the same need. Typing is for producing finished text on a device. Handwriting is for thinking, noting, drafting and sitting exams, and for every situation where a device is absent, banned or inconvenient.

The second objection is that joined writing is harder for some children, particularly those with dyspraxia or other motor difficulties, and that forcing it on them causes distress. This deserves to be taken seriously. But the answer is flexibility, not abolition. Many occupational therapists actually recommend a joined style for some children with motor difficulties, because a continuous movement can be easier to control than repeated stopping and starting, and because it reduces letter reversals such as "b" and "d". Other children will need adaptations, or will move to a keyboard earlier. Good teaching has always made room for individual need. A rule that a few children struggle with a skill is a reason to support those children. It is not a reason to deny everyone else a useful tool.

The third objection is that adults do not really write in cursive anyway. Look at most adults' handwriting, critics say, and you will find a personal hybrid that is partly joined, partly printed, and rarely the textbook loops. This is true, and it is actually an argument for teaching joining. The fluent adult hybrid is what grows out of learning to join. People who were taught to connect letters keep the joins that help them and drop the ones that do not. People who were never taught usually keep a slow, disconnected print that limits how fast they can take notes or write under time pressure. The aim of primary instruction is not to produce adults who write like copybooks. It is to give children a working, efficient hand that they can then make their own.

The fourth objection is that technology will soon make all of this irrelevant. Perhaps one day, but schools should be wary of rebuilding the curriculum around predictions. Exams in many countries are still handwritten. Even where digital assessment is spreading, a lot of thinking still happens on paper: in planning, rough working, sketching ideas and quick notes. Concerns about distraction and about AI-generated work have also pushed some schools and universities back towards handwritten tasks done in class. A child who leaves primary school without fluent handwriting is not being prepared for a digital future. They are being left at a disadvantage in the present.

**Reading as well as writing**

There is a quieter argument that rarely appears in policy debates: children who do not learn to write joined-up often struggle to read it. That might seem minor until you think about what it shuts them out of. Letters from grandparents, notes from teachers, historical documents, family records and a great deal of the handwritten world is joined. In the United States, where cursive teaching declined sharply in the 2010s, archivists and historians raised concerns about a generation unable to read primary sources. Several states, including California in 2023, have since passed laws bringing cursive instruction back. Learning to write a script is the most reliable way to learn to read it. A skill that opens access to the handwritten past and to the people in your own family is not trivial.

**What good teaching looks like**

None of this is a defence of the worst traditions of handwriting teaching: endless copying, marks deducted for imperfect loops, children made to feel stupid because their writing slants the wrong way. Those approaches gave cursive a bad name, and rightly. The case here is for something more modern and more modest.

Children should first learn to form letters correctly, starting in the right place and moving in the right direction, so that joining later comes naturally. Joins should be introduced gradually, starting with the most common letter pairs. Practice should be short, frequent and tied to real writing rather than isolated drills. The goal should be fluency and legibility, not ornament. Typing should be taught alongside, so that children leave primary school able to do both. And children who find joining genuinely hard should get support and alternatives without stigma.

Taught this way, joined-up writing is not a relic. It is the natural end point of learning to handwrite, the stage at which a slow, effortful skill becomes fast enough and automatic enough to serve thinking rather than compete with it.

**Conclusion**

The argument for abandoning joined-up handwriting treats it as decoration, a pleasant extra that a modern curriculum can do without. It is better understood as infrastructure. It makes handwriting fast enough to keep up with thought, it may help children learn and remember, it opens up the handwritten world to them, and it grows into the fluent personal hand that most capable adults use without thinking. Typing matters too, and schools should teach it well. But one does not replace the other. Primary schools that keep teaching children to join their letters are not clinging to the past. They are finishing the job of teaching children to write.
